issues_found: The pack camels central to the caravan and to a defeat condition are represented by SHEEP, although the engine offers Camel Riders and, better still, Trade Carts/Trade Carts-as-caravan for a merchant train; the substitution was avoidable.

Kublai Khan is a renamed GAIA KING — an unowned European monarch figure standing in for the Great Khan, when a Mongol-owned unit (e.g. a renamed Cavalry Archer, Khan, or Genghis Khan-class hero model) would have read far better and could have been placed under the Mongol player.

The Venetian escort is 2 Knights, 2 Men-at-Arms and 2 Crossbowmen — a generic European field detachment rather than the handful of servants and hired local guards a merchant caravan actually travelled with; unit mix would fit any 13th-century engagement.

Elevation is 0 across the entire 120x120 map: the 'mountain passes' of the brief and the Bandit Chief's line 'Merchants, in our pass!' have no corresponding chokepoint or high ground. The scattered CLIFF_DEFAULT_2 and ROCK_FORMATION props are decoration, not terrain.
No water features of consequence (two pinprick tiles), so the Pamir/Oxus river crossings and the scarcity-of-water theme voiced by Niccolo have no map expression.
Narration states the Polos 'depart the port of Hormuz' in 1271; they left Venice in 1271 and only reached Hormuz around 1272 before abandoning the sea route.
Maffeo Polo, Marco's uncle and a co-leader of the actual journey, is absent while the two named villagers cover only Marco and Niccolo.
strengths: Italians for the Venetian caravan and Mongols for the steppe raiders and the Khan's lands are both apt for place and period, and the resulting architecture (Italian tents/pavilion vs. yurts) reads correctly.
The west-to-east terrain gradient from sand to grass steppe genuinely mirrors the Taklamakan/Gobi giving way to the Mongolian grassland, and Marco's line about green steppe is matched by the map.
Victory is gated on bringing the named Marco Polo unit into a specific area at the map's east edge (Shangdu) — exactly the historical objective, not a generic conquest.
Defeat conditions are all specific and historically appropriate: loss of Marco, loss of Niccolo, or loss of the entire pack train, rather than a default 'all units dead'.

Turning points (desert march, ambush at the pass, ambush repelled on the Bandit Chief's death, approach to Shangdu, arrival) fire in order and are gated on player position or kills rather than a clock.
Dates and Marco's age (seventeen in 1271, before the Khan in 1275) match the sources.
justification: The scenario gets the sides, the civilizations and the goal right: Italians escorting two renamed villagers named Marco and Niccolo to a Shangdu arrival area, with defeat on the loss of either Polo or the whole pack train, and a properly ordered chain of position-gated events including an ambush that clears when the Bandit Chief dies. It is undermined by terrain that is entirely flat — elevation 0 on every tile — so the mountain pass the Bandit Chief explicitly claims as 'our pass' does not exist as geography, and by two avoidable casting choices: the caravan's camels are sheep when Trade Carts or Camel Riders were available, and Kublai Khan is a GAIA-owned European KING rather than a Mongol-owned unit. The escort of Knights and Men-at-Arms is a generic period force rather than a merchant train's guard.

Bandit raiders and the Great Khan's own court are both Player 2 (Mongols), so the hostile Karaunas-style brigands and the Khan who is meant to receive the caravan are the same faction.
strengths: Player 1 = Italians is exactly right for a Venetian trading family, and Player 2 = Mongols is right for both the steppe raiders and the Khan's realm.

The terrain digest reproduces the correct west-to-east progression: a broad sand belt across roughly two-thirds of the map giving way to grass steppe in the east, which the D3/D4 dialogue ('the desert gives way to green steppe') explicitly keys off.
Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on the renamed Marco villager at the Shangdu coordinates — the precise historical objective of reaching Kublai Khan's summer court alive.
Defeat conditions are all specific and historically apt: Marco's death, Niccolo's death, or the loss of every pack animal (no provisions, no trade goods); no generic 'lose all units' fallback.
The turning points are gated on player progress and on the Bandit Chief's death rather than on elapsed timers, so the ambush and its repulse follow from what the player does.
Dates and Marco's age (seventeen in 1271, arrival 1275, four years on the road) match the sources.
justification: The scenario gets the framing right — Italians escorting renamed Polo villagers eastward across a correctly graded desert-to-steppe map into Mongol territory, with victory gated on delivering Marco to Shangdu and defeat on the loss of the Polos or the pack animals. It is undermined by two avoidable substitutions: the 'pack camels' are literally sheep when the editor offers Trade Carts and camels, and the 'mountain passes' the brief and objectives both stress are absent from a map whose elevation is entirely flat, gestured at only by 16 cliff props. The escort itself (Knights, Man-at-Arms, Crossbowmen) is interchangeable period filler, and Kublai Khan appears as a Gaia King guarding a European stone castle.

Mongols assigned for the Khan's side, with yurts (YURT_A/B/C) and a Castle standing for the summer palace at Shangdu, is period- and place-correct architecture.
Marco and Niccolo are renamed generic villagers rather than mis-cast heroes — the correct handling, since the engine ships no Polo hero.
Dates and details in the narration check out: departure 1271, Marco aged seventeen (b. 1254), arrival before Kublai in 1275 after four years on the road, Shangdu as the summer court.
The west-to-east desert-to-grass terrain gradient matches the dialogue beat 'the desert gives way to green steppe' and the direction of travel toward the victory area at (102,55)-(112,65).

justification: Civilization assignment is the scenario's strongest element (Italians for Venetians, Mongols for the Khan and steppe raiders), and the win/loss conditions encode exactly the history's stake: Marco alive at Shangdu, versus his death or the loss of the caravan. Against that, the caravan's pack camels are literally SHEEP when Camel Riders and Trade Carts were both available, the escort is generic Castle-age knights and crossbowmen, and Kublai Khan is a European KING model. The map is fatally flat — elevation is 0 on every one of 14,400 tiles, so the 'mountain pass' the ambush dialogue turns on exists only as scattered cliff and rock decorations, though the sand-to-grass gradient does correctly track the route east.

Terrain provides high ground north of a stream that the Norman advance must cross uphill, though the hill is a full-width flat mesa and the water an edge-to-edge band. Events are properly chained rather than timed — advance, feigned retreat, the brothers' fall, then Harold's death — and defeat on William's death or a nightfall deadline encodes exactly the two failures the Normans faced, while the victory condition itself is a bare 1-second timer dependent on the Harold chain.

issues_found: Abd al-Rahman is represented by a CAMEL_RIDER; the Umayyad commander at Tours led horse cavalry, and the engine offered Knight, Mameluke or a renamed generic cavalry unit as better matches. The victory condition therefore hangs on a camel.

Player 1's nine ARCHERs overstate Frankish missile capability — the sources describe an almost purely close-order infantry host of swords, axes and spears; the engine's spearmen/men-at-arms already covered this without archers.
Player THREE (Duke Odo's Aquitanians) holds units and tents but appears in no civilization assignment, so his architecture and unit access are not tied to a Frankish/western civ as they should be.

Elevation is uniformly 0 across the whole 120x120 map. The brief and the narration both turn on Charles Martel occupying 'wooded high ground', the single tactical fact of the battle, and there is no high ground anywhere.

The map is otherwise featureless: a single straight north-south road through undifferentiated oak forest, with no distinction between the Tours and Poitiers ends and no defile or ridge to define the Frankish line.
The two cavalry charges (Battle Begins, Second Charge Wave) fire purely on TIMER, so the Umayyad assault plays out identically regardless of whether the Frankish line is holding or already broken.
strengths: Correct pairing of FRANKS against SARACENS, the closest apt civilizations the engine offers for Charles Martel's host and an Umayyad army out of Iberia.

Force composition inverts correctly: Frankish infantry mass (10 spearmen, 9 men-at-arms, 1 scout) against an all-mounted Umayyad force (12 knights, 8 cavalry archers) with a camp of tents, market and bonfire holding the plunder.
Victory on the death of Abd al-Rahman and defeat on the death of Charles Martel are exactly the two historical hinges — the emir was killed and the Umayyad host dissolved for want of a leader.

Duke Odo's third force is genuinely player-gated: BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA to his hidden western camp, then OBJECTS_IN_AREA when his knights reach the Umayyad baggage, reproducing the raid on the camp that drew horsemen off the line.
Narration dates the battle correctly to October 732 and places it between Tours and Poitiers, and the closing text has the Umayyads withdrawing under cover of night rather than being annihilated.
justification: The scenario gets the sides, the infantry-versus-cavalry asymmetry, and both win/loss conditions right: killing Abd al-Rahman ends it and losing Charles Martel loses it, which is precisely the shape of 732. Its major failure is terrain — the elevation grid is flat zero from edge to edge, so the 'wooded high ground' that the brief, the objectives text and Martel's own dialogue all rest upon simply does not exist, leaving only oak forest and a road. Smaller avoidable errors are the camel-mounted Umayyad emir, nine Frankish archers in a host that fought as a shield-wall, an unassigned civilization for Odo's Aquitanians, and two cavalry charges fired on bare timers rather than on the state of the Frankish line.

issues_found: The narration promises 'Spanish arquebusiers' and Salm's gunpowder-armed garrison, but Player 1 fields only Crossbowmen and Skirmishers; Teutons have access to Hand Cannoneers in the engine, so the omission was avoidable.

Suleiman's 'elite infantry' are generic Champions for the Turks even though the engine ships the Janissary as the Turkish unique unit — the single most identifiable Ottoman troop type at Vienna is absent.

Ottoman force is 3 camel riders, 3 cavalry archers, 4 spearmen, 5 champions and 4 siege pieces — no scale asymmetry at all, whereas Vienna pitted ~20,000 defenders against a vastly larger Ottoman host; the brief's own point about siege cannon being left behind in the mud is contradicted by giving Player 2 two Mangonels and an Onager.

Camel Riders are given prominence (and are the victory trigger object) though camelry was marginal in the 1529 Vienna campaign; Ottoman sipahi cavalry would be better served by the Cavalry Archer/light cavalry already present.

Terrain is entirely flat (elevation all zeros) with no representation of Vienna's ditch, glacis or the ruined Carinthian bastion; the walled dirt square is a featureless rectangle rather than the city's actual circuit.
The Danube appears only as an undifferentiated water band along the top five rows — no island, arm, or bridgehead, and no relation to the Ottoman approach up the river described in the intro.
Victory is gated on destroying a single Camel Rider, which encodes 'kill one enemy horseman' rather than 'outlast the siege until the autumn withdrawal'.
Defeat on the death of the Salm Champion asserts that the garrison collapses without him, whereas historically Salm was mortally wounded during the siege and Vienna still held.
strengths: Civilizations are exactly right: Teutons for the German Landsknecht garrison of the Empire, Turks for Suleiman's Ottomans.
Salm is a renamed generic unit and Suleiman a renamed King — correct handling, since the engine ships no hero for either figure.
The stone-wall circuit with a single gate, Castle, Guard Towers and Town Center inside a dirt-terrain city gives a genuine defensive chokepoint for the Carinthian Gate fighting.

The mine/countermine episode is genuinely interactive: a BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA branch detonates the mine and breaches the gate, while a DESTROY_OBJECT branch on the sapping engine collapses the tunnel — the historical countermining duel rendered as a player choice.
Text is chronologically accurate: September 1529, the Danube approach, the heavy siege artillery bogged down in autumn mud, reliance on sappers, and withdrawal forced by rain and supply failure.
Assault waves escalate in order (sappers, spearmen/horse-archers, final elite push) with each later stage chained via ACTIVATE_TRIGGER off the previous one's resolution.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right — Teutons versus Turks, renamed Salm and Suleiman, a walled city with a single contested gate, and narration that is factually sound about 1529, the mud-bound siege guns, the sapping war, and the rain-and-supply withdrawal — and its mine/countermine branch is real interactivity rather than a timed cutscene. It is undermined by an avoidable roster: no Janissaries for the Ottoman elite infantry the text explicitly names, no Hand Cannoneers for the Spanish arquebusiers the text explicitly names, Ottoman siege artillery present despite the dialogue saying it lagged behind, and no numerical asymmetry between garrison and horde. Terrain is a flat rectangle with the Danube shoved to the map edge and zero elevation or outworks, and victory is gated on killing one Camel Rider rather than on surviving to the withdrawal, so the encoded goal only loosely matches the endurance problem the defenders actually faced.
